_meta.purpose: What each identifier on tokenization.systems says and means, for editors replacing numbers in reader-visible text with words. Each entry: plain (a phrase usable in a sentence), says (one sentence on what it says or does), source (where it was read). Aliases are other spellings of the same identifier. A context field means the same number means something else elsewhere: read the page before choosing an entry. A note flags something to correct or confirm.

RIN 1505-AC90.plain: Treasury's proposed principles for deciding when a state stablecoin regime is substantially similar to the federal one
RIN 1505-AC90.says: Would set broad-based principles for determining when a state-level regulatory regime for payment stablecoin issuers is substantially similar to the federal framework.

RIN 1505-AC95.plain: Treasury's proposed rule on who may issue payment stablecoins and who may offer or sell them

31 U.S.C. 5318(h)(5).says: The duty to establish, maintain and enforce a program must be performed by persons in the United States accessible to, and overseen by, the Treasury and the appropriate federal functional regulator.

31 U.S.C. 5312(a)(2)(Y).plain: the Bank Secrecy Act's catch-all definition of a financial institution
31 U.S.C. 5312(a)(2)(Y).says: Includes as a financial institution any business Treasury determines by regulation engages in an activity similar to, related to, or a substitute for those of the listed businesses.

12 U.S.C. 5903(e).plain: the GENIUS Act's rule that payment stablecoins are not federally insured and may not be represented as insured
12 U.S.C. 5903(e).says: Section 4(e): payment stablecoins are not backed by the United States or federally insured, and it is unlawful to represent otherwise.

12 U.S.C. 5903(c).plain: the GENIUS Act's option for smaller issuers to be regulated by a state
12 U.S.C. 5903(c).says: Section 4(c): a state qualified issuer with no more than $10 billion in consolidated total outstanding issuance may opt for a state regime that is substantially similar to the federal framework.

12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(6)(B).plain: the GENIUS Act's requirement that issuers be able to comply with lawful orders
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(6)(B).says: Section 4(a)(6)(B): the issuer's technological capability to comply with lawful orders.

12 U.S.C. 5901(16)(B).plain: the part of the GENIUS Act's definition of a lawful order that names accounts
12 U.S.C. 5901(16)(B).says: A lawful order must specify the payment stablecoins or accounts subject to blocking with reasonable particularity.

12 U.S.C. 5907.plain: the GENIUS Act's anti-money-laundering protections against noncompliant foreign issuers
12 U.S.C. 5907.says: Section 8: Treasury may designate a foreign issuer that fails to comply with a lawful order as noncompliant and prohibit secondary trading of its stablecoin.

Pub. L. 119-27.says: The Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins Act, signed into law July 18, 2025.

section 3 (GENIUS Act).plain: the GENIUS Act's limits on who may issue, offer and sell payment stablecoins
section 3 (GENIUS Act).says: Makes it unlawful for anyone but a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to issue a payment stablecoin in the United States, and from July 18, 2028 limits what digital asset service providers may offer or sell.
section 3 (GENIUS Act).context: GENIUS Act; letters hub, tracker, Treasury letters, notes, resumes

section 3(b)(1).says: From three years after enactment, a digital asset service provider may offer or sell a payment stablecoin to a person in the United States only if a permitted payment stablecoin issuer issued it, subject to exceptions.

section 3(b)(2).plain: the GENIUS Act's condition on foreign issuers' stablecoins
section 3(b)(2).says: A digital asset service provider may not make a foreign issuer's payment stablecoin available in the United States unless the issuer has the technological capability to comply, and will comply, with lawful orders and any reciprocal arrangement.

section 4 (GENIUS Act).plain: the GENIUS Act's requirements for issuers
section 4 (GENIUS Act).says: Sets the standards for issuing payment stablecoins, including reserves, redemption, permitted activities and state regimes.

Section 4(a)(11).plain: the GENIUS Act's ban on issuers paying holders interest or yield
Section 4(a)(11).says: No permitted or foreign payment stablecoin issuer may pay a holder any form of interest or yield solely for holding, using or retaining the stablecoin.

sections 4(a)(5) and 4(a)(6)(B).plain: the GENIUS Act's Bank Secrecy Act and lawful-order requirements
sections 4(a)(5) and 4(a)(6)(B).says: An issuer is treated as a financial institution under the Bank Secrecy Act and must have the technological capability to comply with lawful orders.

Section 4(a)(7)(B).plain: the GENIUS Act's rule on incidental activities
Section 4(a)(7)(B).says: The list of permitted activities does not stop an issuer from activities the regulator authorizes that the Act specifies, and those incidental to them.

Section 4(a)(7)(A).plain: the GENIUS Act's list of what an issuer may do
Section 4(a)(7)(A).says: An issuer may only issue and redeem payment stablecoins, manage related reserves, provide custody for stablecoins, reserves or private keys, and undertake activities that directly support those.

section 4(c).plain: the GENIUS Act's provisions for state regimes
section 4(c).says: Lets a smaller state qualified issuer opt for a state regime that is substantially similar to the federal framework, with state regulators certifying that to the Stablecoin Certification Review Committee.

Section 5 (GENIUS Act).plain: the GENIUS Act's approval process for issuers
Section 5 (GENIUS Act).says: Sets how an applicant, including a bank's subsidiary, applies to its federal regulator for approval and what the regulator weighs.

§5(c)(5).plain: the regulator's power under the GENIUS Act to add approval factors
§5(c)(5).says: Lets the primary federal regulator establish other factors necessary to ensure the safety and soundness of the issuer.

Section 6 (GENIUS Act).plain: the GENIUS Act's supervision and enforcement provisions
Section 6 (GENIUS Act).says: Sets how federal regulators supervise and enforce against federal qualified issuers and bank subsidiaries.

section 6(b).says: Lets the regulator suspend or revoke an issuer's registration and prohibit it from issuing payment stablecoins in stated cases.

section 7(f)(4).plain: the GENIUS Act's carve-out for state consumer protection laws
section 7(f)(4).says: Apart from state chartering and licensing laws, nothing in the Act preempts state consumer protection laws.

section 8.plain: the GENIUS Act's anti-money-laundering protections against noncompliant foreign issuers
section 8.says: Section 8: Treasury may designate a foreign issuer that fails to comply with a lawful order as noncompliant and prohibit secondary trading of its stablecoin.

section 8(b).plain: the GENIUS Act's secondary trading prohibition
section 8(b).says: If a foreign issuer does not comply within 30 days of notice, Treasury publishes the determination and a prohibition on facilitating secondary trading, which takes effect 30 days after notification.

§11.plain: the GENIUS Act's treatment of issuers in insolvency
§11.says: Section 11 sets holders' priority in an issuer's insolvency, including an amendment to the Bankruptcy Code's priority rules.

Section 507.says: Section 507 of title 11, which the GENIUS Act amends to give holders priority in an issuer's bankruptcy.

Section 13.says: Regulators and Treasury must issue implementing regulations within one year of enactment, through notice and comment.

section 18.plain: the GENIUS Act's conditions for foreign issuers
section 18.says: A foreign issuer is excepted from the section 3 prohibitions if, among other things, it is regulated under a regime Treasury finds comparable, is registered with the OCC, and holds enough reserves in a United States financial institution.

Section 20.says: The Act takes effect on the earlier of 18 months after enactment or 120 days after the primary federal regulators issue final regulations.

§350.4.plain: the FDIC's proposed reserve asset requirements
§350.4.says: Requires identifiable reserves fully backing the stablecoin and sets what they may hold, how concentrated they may be and how they are reported.
§350.4.note: The fdic-ag19-ppsi-activities page calls §350.4 the "capital framework". In the proposed rule section 350.4 is reserve assets; capital is at sections 350.8 through 350.10. Correct this when the page is edited.

§350.4(f).plain: the FDIC's proposed 40 percent cap on reserve exposure to any one institution
§350.4(f).says: An issuer must limit its exposure to any one eligible financial institution to no more than 40 percent of its reserve assets on each business day.

§350.6(b).plain: the FDIC's proposed information technology and security program
§350.6(b).says: Requires a program for information technology and security risks, including secure handling of digital assets and private key management, backup and recovery.

§350.7(g).plain: the FDIC's proposed confidential weekly report
§350.7(g).says: Every issuer must send the FDIC a confidential weekly report containing the information the FDIC specifies.

§330.11(a)(3).plain: the FDIC's proposed bar on pass-through deposit insurance for stablecoin reserves
§330.11(a)(3).says: Deposits held as reserves for a payment stablecoin would be insured as corporate deposits of the issuer, not passed through to stablecoin holders.

§330.1(e).plain: the FDIC's proposed technology-neutral change to the definition of deposit account records
§330.1(e).says: An insured bank's choice of technology or recordkeeping would not affect deposit insurance coverage.

§330.3(k).plain: the FDIC's proposed rule on technology used to record deposits
§330.3(k).says: The technology or recordkeeping a bank uses to record deposit liabilities would not affect whether they are deposits.

§303.252.plain: the FDIC's proposed application rule for stablecoin-issuing subsidiaries
§303.252.says: Sets the application requirements and procedures for an FDIC-supervised bank seeking approval for a subsidiary to issue payment stablecoins.

§303.252(d)(1).plain: the application's description of the proposed stablecoin and activities
§303.252(d)(1).says: Requires a description of the proposed stablecoin, the subsidiary's proposed activities, related activities of the applicant, and how the stablecoin's value will be kept stable.

§303.252(d)(2).plain: the application's financial information, including the reserve asset management plan
§303.252(d)(2).says: Requires financial information including capital and liquidity, reserve assets and an associated asset management plan, and three years of projections.

§303.252(d)(4).plain: the application's policies, procedures and customer agreements
§303.252(d)(4).says: Requires policies, procedures and customer agreements covering custody, segregation, recordkeeping, redemption, and anti-money-laundering and sanctions requirements.

Section 350.6(d).plain: the FDIC's proposed Bank Secrecy Act and sanctions compliance requirement
Section 350.6(d).says: Each issuer must comply with the Bank Secrecy Act, the GENIUS Act's related sections, and OFAC and FinCEN regulations, including program and reporting requirements.

Section 350.200.plain: the definitions in the FDIC's proposed anti-money-laundering supervision rules
Section 350.200.says: Defines terms such as anti-money-laundering enforcement action and significant supervisory action.

Section 350.201.plain: the FDIC's proposed anti-money-laundering supervision and enforcement policy
Section 350.201.says: An issuer that has established an effective program will not face an enforcement or significant supervisory action, except for a significant or systemic failure to implement it.

Section 350.202.plain: the FDIC's proposed consultation with FinCEN
Section 350.202.says: Before an enforcement action or significant supervisory action, the FDIC gives the FinCEN Director a chance to review it and considers any input.

Section 350.202(b)(1).plain: the FDIC's proposed 30-day notice to FinCEN
Section 350.202(b)(1).says: The FDIC sends FinCEN written notice at least 30 days before acting, with the relevant information, unless a shorter period is needed.

Section 350.203.plain: the FDIC's proposed options for sharing supervisory information with FinCEN
Section 350.203.says: Sets options for disclosure to FinCEN of information about an existing or potential action.

Section 19.260.plain: the definitions in the OCC's proposed anti-money-laundering supervision rules
Section 19.260.says: Defines terms such as anti-money-laundering enforcement action.

Section 19.261.plain: the OCC's proposed consultation with FinCEN
Section 19.261.says: Before an enforcement action or significant supervisory action, the OCC gives the FinCEN Director a chance to review it and considers any input.

Section 19.261(b).plain: the OCC's proposed 30-day notice to FinCEN
Section 19.261(b).says: The OCC sends FinCEN written notice at least 30 days before acting, with the relevant information, unless a shorter period is needed.

Section 19.262.plain: the OCC's proposed anti-money-laundering enforcement and supervision policy
Section 19.262.says: An issuer that has established an effective program will not face an enforcement or significant supervisory action, except for a significant or systemic failure to implement it.

Section 15.13(c).plain: the OCC's proposed Bank Secrecy Act and sanctions compliance requirement
Section 15.13(c).says: Each issuer must comply with the Bank Secrecy Act, the GENIUS Act's related sections, and OFAC and FinCEN regulations, including program and reporting requirements.

Section 15.11.says: Requires an issuer to maintain identifiable reserve assets and sets what they may be.

Section 15.13.says: Sets operational and managerial standards for an issuer, including internal controls.

Section 4.19.plain: the OCC's proposed rule on disclosing supervisory information to FinCEN
Section 4.19.says: Governs disclosure to FinCEN of supervisory information about permitted payment stablecoin issuers.

Section 706.202(c).plain: the NCUA's proposed reserve diversification and concentration standard
Section 706.202(c).says: An issuer must keep reserves diverse enough to manage credit, liquidity, interest rate and price risks, and manage concentration at any one institution.

Section 706.202(e).plain: the NCUA's proposed reserve composition report
Section 706.202(e).says: Requires a report on the composition of an issuer's reserve assets, and allows surplus reserves to be withdrawn only after the month-end report is examined and certified.

Section 706.203.says: An issuer must publicly disclose its redemption policy, including how quickly it will redeem.

Section 208.63.plain: the Federal Reserve's proposed anti-money-laundering program rule for state member banks
Section 208.63.says: Would require Federal Reserve-supervised banks to establish and maintain effective anti-money-laundering and countering the financing of terrorism programs.

Section 208.63(a).plain: the definitions in the Federal Reserve's proposed anti-money-laundering rule
Section 208.63(a).says: Defines terms including enforcement action and significant supervisory action.

Section 208.63(c)(1)(i)(A).plain: the Federal Reserve's proposed risk assessment of business activities
Section 208.63(c)(1)(i)(A).says: A bank's risk assessment must evaluate its business activities, including products, services, distribution channels, customers and geographic locations.

Section 208.63(c)(1)(i)(C).plain: the Federal Reserve's proposed requirement to update risk assessments promptly
Section 208.63(c)(1)(i)(C).says: A bank must update its risk assessment promptly on any change it knows or has reason to know significantly changes its risks.

Section 208.63(e).plain: the Federal Reserve's proposed written program and approval requirement
Section 208.63(e).says: A bank's program must be written and approved by its board, an equivalent governing body or appropriate senior management.

Section 208.63(g).plain: the Federal Reserve's proposed enforcement and supervision policy
Section 208.63(g).says: A bank that has established a program will not face an enforcement or significant supervisory action related to implementation, except for a significant or systemic failure.

Section 208.63(c)(2).plain: the Federal Reserve's proposed independent testing requirement
Section 208.63(c)(2).says: A bank's program must include independent testing.

Section 208.63(c)(3).plain: the Federal Reserve's proposed anti-money-laundering officer requirement
Section 208.63(c)(3).says: A bank must designate an individual located in the United States, accessible to and overseen by FinCEN and the Board, to run the program.

Sections 360.10(b).plain: the definitions in the FDIC's proposed resolution submission rule
Sections 360.10(b).says: Defines terms including which insured banks are covered.

Section 327.18.plain: the FDIC's proposed Resolution Readiness Adjustment
Section 327.18.says: A downward adjustment to assessment rates for large or highly complex institutions that elect to show resolution readiness.

Section 309.37.plain: the FDIC's proposed rule on disclosure by insured banks and other entities
Section 309.37.says: Sets when insured banks and certain other entities may disclose confidential information.

§1521.plain: Treasury's proposed principles for substantially similar state regimes
§1521.says: Would set broad-based principles for determining when a state-level regulatory regime for payment stablecoin issuers is substantially similar to the federal framework.

§1521.2(b)(1).plain: Treasury's overall test for a substantially similar state regime
§1521.2(b)(1).says: A state regime must meet or exceed the federal standards, with uniform requirements consistent in all substantive respects and state-calibrated ones leading to outcomes at least as stringent and protective.

§1521.3.plain: Treasury's principles for the uniform requirements
§1521.3.says: Uniform requirements must be fully enforceable by the state regulator and consistent with the federal framework.

§1521.5.plain: Treasury's principles for other GENIUS Act provisions
§1521.5.says: Covers state regime provisions on transition to federal oversight, custody, insolvency and related matters.

§1521.6.plain: Treasury's principles for additional state requirements
§1521.6.says: A state may impose additional requirements if they do not conflict with the Act, the rule or federal law.

Sec. 1523.1.plain: the scope and definitions in Treasury's proposed issuance rule
Sec. 1523.1.says: Sets the scope of the rule and defines its terms.

Sec. 1523.1(c).plain: the definitions in Treasury's proposed issuance rule
Sec. 1523.1(c).says: Defines terms, taking digital asset service provider and lawful order from the GENIUS Act.

Sec. 1523.2(c).plain: Treasury's proposed rule on issuing outside the United States
Sec. 1523.2(c).says: A person is deemed not to issue in the United States if it is outside the country, reasonably believes each recipient is too, and has controls to avoid issuing to anyone in the United States.

Sec. 1523.3(c).plain: Treasury's proposed rule on relying on a foreign issuer's representation
Sec. 1523.3(c).says: A digital asset service provider may rely on a foreign issuer's representation that it can and will comply with lawful orders only after reasonable due diligence, and not where it knows, has reason to know, or should know otherwise.

Sec. 1523.3(e).plain: Treasury's proposed rule on offers and sales outside the United States
Sec. 1523.3(e).says: A provider is deemed not to offer or sell in the United States if it reasonably believes the person is not located there and has controls to avoid it.

§1033.210.plain: FinCEN's proposed anti-money-laundering program requirement for stablecoin issuers
§1033.210.says: Sets the required elements of an issuer's anti-money-laundering and countering the financing of terrorism program.

§1033.240.plain: FinCEN's proposed block, freeze and reject requirement
§1033.240.says: An issuer must have the technical capabilities, policies and procedures to block, freeze and reject impermissible transactions and to comply with any lawful order.
§1033.240.note: The letters hub called this a GENIUS Act section. It is a section of the proposed FinCEN rule.

§1010.100(rrr).plain: FinCEN's proposed definition of a lawful order
§1010.100(rrr).says: Defines lawful order as in the GENIUS Act, with changes in light of an existing FinCEN definition; the term names the stablecoins or accounts subject to blocking.

§1010.100(ff)(8)(iii).plain: FinCEN's proposed exclusion of stablecoin issuers from the definition of a money services business
§1010.100(ff)(8)(iii).says: Adds permitted payment stablecoin issuers to the entities excluded from the definition.

§502.201(b).plain: OFAC's proposed sanctions compliance program requirement
§502.201(b).says: Sets five elements: senior management commitment, risk assessment, internal controls, testing and auditing, and training.

Section 1033.100(a).plain: the proposed definition of an account for customer identification
Section 1033.100(a).says: An account is a formal relationship between a customer and an issuer, and excludes activity that does not directly involve the issuer other than via a smart contract.

Section 1033.100(a)(1).plain: the proposed list of relationships that make an account
Section 1033.100(a)(1).says: Lists issuing or redeeming, managing reserves, custody, supporting activities, and providing digital asset service provider services.

Section 1033.100(a)(1)(v).plain: the proposed account definition's digital asset service provider item
Section 1033.100(a)(1)(v).says: Reads: Providing services of a digital asset service provider.

Sections 1033.100(b)(2)(iv).plain: the proposed exclusion from the definition of a customer for buyers who do not deal with the issuer
Sections 1033.100(b)(2)(iv).says: A person acquiring or redeeming a payment stablecoin other than directly from or to the issuer is not a customer.

Section 1033.220(c).plain: the proposed clause preserving other obligations, including lawful orders
Section 1033.220(c).says: Nothing in the customer identification section relieves an issuer of its other obligations, including complying with lawful orders.

Section 1033.220(a)(2)(ii).says: A program must verify each customer's identity within a reasonable time before or after the account is opened.

Section 1033.220(a)(4).plain: the proposed comparison with government lists
Section 1033.220(a)(4).says: A program must determine whether a customer appears on any federal list of known or suspected terrorists or terrorist organizations that Treasury designates for this purpose.

Section 1033.220(a)(6).says: A program may rely on another financial institution's performance of its procedures on stated conditions.

section 1010.668(a)(1).plain: the proposed definition of the A7 Network
section 1010.668(a)(1).says: Defines the A7 Network as the core group of entities and persons running a Russian-Kyrgyzstan based sanctions evasion and money laundering network.

section 1010.668(a)(4).plain: the proposed definition of a covered financial institution
section 1010.668(a)(4).says: Uses the same meaning as financial institution in FinCEN's general regulations.

section 1010.668(b)(1)(i).plain: the proposed safe harbor for receiving funds from a Sub-Agent
section 1010.668(b)(1)(i).says: An institution is deemed not to violate the ban if, on finding it received convertible virtual currency from a Sub-Agent, it blocks the funds where required or rejects and returns them.

Rule 400.plain: the SEC's proposed safe harbor for when a crypto asset stops being subject to an investment contract
Rule 400.says: A covered investment contract is deemed to have ceased, and the crypto asset no longer subject to it, if the issuer has completed or permanently ceased its promised essential managerial efforts and files a transition report.

Rule 400(a).says: The issuer has completed or permanently ceased all essential managerial efforts it represented or promised, and is not making and does not intend to make new such promises.

Rule 400(b).says: The issuer files a transition report containing the information Form TR requires.

Form TR.says: The report an issuer would file to rely on the safe harbor, with a description, a certification and a supporting analysis.

Rule 103.plain: the proposed disclosure rule in Regulation Crypto Assets
Rule 103.says: Sets general disclosure principles and the information an issuer must disclose under the exemptions.

Rule 103(b)(1).plain: the proposed requirement to disclose the issuer's promises and progress
Rule 103(b)(1).says: An issuer must describe the material terms of the investment contract, including its promises to engage in essential managerial efforts and its progress on them.

Rule 100.plain: the proposed definitions in Regulation Crypto Assets
Rule 100.says: Defines terms including related person: founders, promoters, employees, affiliates, directors, officers, trustees, consultants, contractors, advisors and their immediate family.

Section 2(a)(1).plain: the Securities Act's definition of a security
Section 2(a)(1).says: The Securities Act of 1933 definition the safe harbor refers to.

Section 3(a)(10).plain: the Exchange Act's definition of a security
Section 3(a)(10).says: The Securities Exchange Act of 1934 definition the safe harbor refers to.

section 36(a)(1).plain: the SEC's general exemptive authority under the Exchange Act
section 36(a)(1).says: Lets the Commission exempt persons or transactions from the Exchange Act by order, on stated findings.

section 3(a)(1).plain: the Exchange Act's definition of an exchange
section 3(a)(1).says: The definition the Order exempts qualifying venues from.

section 3(a)(5).plain: the Exchange Act's definition of a dealer
section 3(a)(5).says: The definition the Order exempts certain liquidity providers from.

Section 15(a).plain: the Exchange Act's broker-dealer registration requirement
Section 15(a).says: The requirement that the SEC staff statement on Covered User Interface Providers says a provider meeting twelve conditions need not be treated as subject to.

Release No. 34-106402.plain: the SEC's order on tokenized stock trading venues and liquidity providers
Release No. 34-106402.says: An order exempting certain distributed ledger trading venues for tokenized national market system stock from the definition of exchange, and certain liquidity providers from the definition of dealer, from September 17, 2026 until September 17, 2031.

Release No. 34-106246.plain: the SEC's proposal on transfer agent rules
Release No. 34-106246.says: Would adopt new rules, amend existing rules and amend Forms TA-1 and TA-2 to modernize the rules governing registered transfer agents.

Release Nos. 33-11434 and 34-106150.plain: the SEC's proposal of Regulation Crypto Assets
Release Nos. 33-11434 and 34-106150.says: Would create a tailored offering regime for investment contracts involving crypto assets, with startup and fundraising exemptions, disclosure requirements and a safe harbor.

34-105047.plain: the SEC's order letting Nasdaq trade securities in tokenized form
34-105047.says: An order approving Nasdaq's rule change to enable the trading of securities on the exchange in tokenized form, published March 23, 2026.

OMB control number 3038-0076.plain: the CFTC's information collection for derivatives clearing organizations
OMB control number 3038-0076.says: The notice proposing to renew the collection of reporting requirements for derivatives clearing organizations under the Paperwork Reduction Act.

Section 404 (CLARITY Act).plain: the Senate-stage CLARITY Act's parallel ban on service providers paying yield
Section 404 (CLARITY Act).says: The Senate-stage print of the CLARITY Act would extend a prohibition parallel to the GENIUS Act's to digital asset service providers and their affiliates; pending, not law.

Section 529.says: A section 529 plan is a tax-advantaged savings plan for education costs under the Internal Revenue Code; the frameworks page cites these plans as an analogy.

DGCL § 224.plain: Delaware's corporate law provision on keeping stock ledgers
DGCL § 224.says: A corporation's records, including its stock ledger, may be kept on electronic networks or databases, including distributed ones.

UCC Article 12.plain: the Uniform Commercial Code's rules for digital assets
UCC Article 12.says: Sets rules for controllable electronic records, including the take-free protection for a qualifying purchaser.

UCC Article 4A.plain: the Uniform Commercial Code's funds-transfer article
UCC Article 4A.says: Sets rules for funds transfers, including when payment is final.

Staff Letter 25-39.plain: the CFTC staff's letter on tokenized collateral
Staff Letter 25-39.says: Three CFTC divisions' views on using tokenized assets as collateral; staff-level guidance that does not bind the Commission.

Regulation 39.13(g).plain: the CFTC's margin rule for clearing organizations
Regulation 39.13(g).says: Sets initial margin requirements, including the assets accepted, haircuts and concentration limits, the latter two evaluated at least monthly.

Regulation 39.27(b).plain: the CFTC's legal risk rule for clearing organizations
Regulation 39.27(b).says: Requires a well-founded, enforceable legal framework, including the unimpeded ability to liquidate collateral on a clearing member's default.

USA PATRIOT Act section 314(a).plain: FinCEN's information requests to financial institutions on behalf of law enforcement
USA PATRIOT Act section 314(a).says: FinCEN's proposal treats responding to these requests as part of how an issuer shares information and informs its risk assessment.

Section 2 (Seven Dollars).plain: the Seven Dollars section on its four-dimension taxonomy
Section 2 (Seven Dollars).says: Classifies the seven products along four dimensions.

Section 3 (Seven Dollars).plain: the Seven Dollars section extending the CLII
Section 3 (Seven Dollars).says: Extends the Control Layer Intensity Index to the paper's products.

Section 3.2 (Seven Dollars).plain: the Seven Dollars section on the US-holder design axis
Section 3.2 (Seven Dollars).says: Tabulates five design markers across eleven products and sorts them by whether they are built for US holders.

Section 4 (Seven Dollars).plain: the Seven Dollars section applying the MVEP
Section 4 (Seven Dollars).says: Applies the MVEP to the seven products.
Section 4 (Seven Dollars).note: The paper page labels eligibility composites "Collateral eligibility (Section 4)". In the manuscript that framework is section 7 and section 4 is The MVEP Applied. Name the topic, not the number.

Section 5 (Seven Dollars).plain: the Seven Dollars section on dependency mapping and contagion
Section 5 (Seven Dollars).says: Maps dependencies among the products and how stress spread in observed episodes.

Section 6 (Seven Dollars).plain: the Seven Dollars section on the Silicon Valley Bank counterfactual
Section 6 (Seven Dollars).says: Compares concentration points across the products before and after the Silicon Valley Bank failure.

Section 6.7.plain: the Seven Dollars section on PYUSD's operational risk
Section 6.7.says: The section titled PYUSD: Operational Risk in Production.

Section 7.2.plain: the Seven Dollars collateral eligibility results
Section 7.2.says: Reports the published eligibility composites and tiers per product.

Sections 3, 7.2, and 7.3.plain: the Seven Dollars tables on the CLII and collateral eligibility
Sections 3, 7.2, and 7.3.says: The source tables for the page's chart.

Section 7.3.plain: the Seven Dollars robustness exhibit on collateral eligibility
Section 7.3.says: Scores the same metrics with one explicit rule per metric.

Sections 2, 4, 5, and 9 (Three Strategie.plain: the Three Strategies sections on the infrastructure map, stress scenarios, Securitize concentration and the MVEP application
Sections 2, 4, 5, and 9 (Three Strategie.says: The sources for the page's dependency matrix.

Section 3.1.plain: the Three Strategies section on the Regulated Collateral Circuit

Section 3.2 (Three Strategies).plain: the Three Strategies section on the Multi-Issuer Yield Stack

Section 3.3.plain: the Three Strategies section on the Tokenized Equity Rails

Section 5 (Three Strategies).plain: the Three Strategies section on Securitize concentration risk
Section 5 (Three Strategies).says: Examines Securitize's role as transfer agent in all three strategies.

Section 6 (Three Strategies).plain: the Three Strategies section on the corporate actions reconciliation gap
Section 6 (Three Strategies).says: Examines how corporate actions reconcile under around-the-clock trading.

Section 6.2.plain: the Three Strategies section on three reconciliation architectures
Section 6.2.says: Sets out three architectures for reconciling corporate actions.

Section 8 (Three Strategies).plain: the Three Strategies section on phase gates
Section 8 (Three Strategies).says: Sets observable milestones for each strategy transition.

Section 8 (Adaptive Tokenomics).plain: the Adaptive Tokenomics section on what simulation reveals
